newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - US debt vols soften as bonds bounce back.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - US debt vols soften as bonds bounce back.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. debt options were softer across the board in late trade as underlying fixed-income markets bounced back from Friday's losses, dealers said.
They said fears of a Federal Reserve credit tightening -- provoked last week by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's warnings on "irrational exuberance" in asset markets -- appeared to be abating.
"It (volatility) has gradually come off, and it seems to me like it's taking the day out," said a Treasury bond trader at a brokerage firm at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).
Implied volatility for CBOT March T-bond futures options slid about 0.1 point to around 9.8 percent.

March futures were up 15/32 on the day at 114-10/32 in late trade, already back above Thursday's close of 114-3/32, which was before the Greenspan comments. Late Thursday evening, Greenspan said the Fed must be wary when "irrational exuberance" infected asset markets.
Traders said the market was now awaiting Wednesday's November U.S. producer price index and Thursday's consumer price index.
They said bonds were likely to regain confidence and resume its bull trend, pressuring implied volatilities, if the prices data turned out to be benign as expected.
Volatilities at the shorter end of the yield curve were also weaker as the underlying market, which had suffered less than bonds during Friday's early selloff, was firmer.
"I think the long end of the market is the primary mover and we're going to be lagging a little bit," said a Eurodollar options trader for a brokerage firm at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME).
Implied volatilities for March Eurodollar futures options slipped 0.3 point to 10.1 percent and June dropped a little more than half a point to 13.7 percent.
"The problem is that we are already getting to pretty low levels," the CME trader said, noting that this could lead to a period of stagnation in options trading.

He said even if the underlying market starts to calm down going into the holiday season, option traders would become reluctant to take on short volatility positions because of the relatively small premiums they would receive.
Among the few sizeable deals done today, an investment bank was seen buying 1,000 legs each of January, February and March 94.25/94.50 call spreads in a two-by-three ratio.
A European bank affiliate was said to have bought 2,000 lots of 94.00 straddles in short March contracts, which are options expiring in March 1997 but based on March 1997 futures.
